meaning: the god of fire, the fire of the stomach, digestive faculty, gastric fluid

phonemes.desc: The a is the open “ah”; g is a hard stop. The name IS the common noun “fire”.
Palatal n with a long ī in Vedic lengthening; the word carries its own glow.

pronunciation.note: His name is cognate with Latin ignis: the god and the element share one root across three millennia.

domains.title: God of Fire, the Sacrifice, the Messenger
domains.subtitle: The Priest of the Gods and the Guest of Men
domains.lead: Agni is fire worshipped as a god: the flame that carries every offering upward, the guest in every home’s hearth, the priest of the gods and the god of priests. Second only to Indra in Vedic hymns, he is the most frequently invoked deity at the ritual itself — for without Agni, no prayer reaches heaven.

cards.name: The Messenger
cards.desc: Every offering is carried to the gods through his flame — Agni is the one channel of prayer.

cards.name: Threefold Fire
cards.desc: He has three births — in the heavens as sun, in the waters as lightning, on earth as the hearth-flame.

cards.name: The Divine Priest
cards.desc: Hotṛ of the gods, he conducts the rite he is offered at — god and officiant in one flame.

cards.name: Consumer and Purifier
cards.desc: He eats the oblation and burns away sin; the dead pass through his mouth to the fathers.

mythology.lead: Agni’s mythology is less narrative than elemental: he is born daily from the friction-sticks, devours his parents (the sticks that bore him) at birth, and carries the sacrifice skyward. Yet the Vedic poets gave him a full biography — hidden at birth, stolen by the gods, established among men — and the epics gave him a genealogy and a role in every hero’s fire-drill.

myths.title: The Hidden Birth
myths.text: The birth-hymns tell that Agni was concealed in the waters and the wood, secret like a son hidden by his mother, until the ten sisters — the fingers of the kindling-priest — rubbed him forth. ‘The new-born infant licks the earth’: the first flame tasting the world it will consume and consecrate.

myths.title: Agni Flees the Sacrifice
myths.text: In the great dialogue hymn, Agni hides from the burden of the office — the god who must eat the offering shrinks from being eaten by his own hunger. The gods find him in the waters, the fig-tree, the plants; each offers to hide him; he returns to the ritual because prayer without fire goes nowhere. It is the most psychologically modern of Vedic hymns.

myths.title: The Stolen Fire of the Gods
myths.text: The Brāhmaṇas narrate how the gods kept Agni from men until Mātariśvan, the Vedic Prometheus, brought him down hidden in the stalk of a plant — the mythic warrant for the fire-drill itself, and for the conviction that fire is heaven’s property on loan to the hearth.

myths.title: Agni and the Khandava Forest
myths.text: In the epic, Agni, weakened by a surfeit of ghee, begs Krishna and Arjuna to let him burn the Khandava forest; fed by the conflagration, he blazes up again as of old. The episode fixes the epic’s theology of fire: indiscriminate when ravenous, a god still, and the friend of heroes who understand his hunger.

lore.syncretism: Agni is the Vedic counterpart of the Avestan Atar, and the fire-cult is the one element Zoroastrianism kept most fully from the old Indo-Iranian religion. Greek writers compared him to Hephaestus and the altar-flame; modern linguistics binds him to Latin ignis and English ignite. In Hindu ritual he remains unpolluted by sect — every saṃskāra from birth to cremation passes through him.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Agnihotra — the twice-daily milk-offering to fire — has been performed continuously for three thousand years and is still performed today, the oldest uninterrupted ritual on earth. His name, through Latin ignis, kindled the English language’s whole fire-vocabulary; and the ritual fire’s three forms shaped the theology of light in every Indian tradition.
lore.extendedMeditation: Agni: the god whose name is a common noun across four language families. Restoring him in ASCII requires no scholarship at all — every reader has already said his name a thousand times, in ‘ignite’, in ‘ignition’, in the strike of a match. He is the most restored god in the lexicon because his restoration is involuntary.
lore.archaeology: The fire-altar itself is his monument: the brick agnicayana altars of the Śrauta ritual, rebuilt in every performance to the geometry the Śulbasūtras prescribe. Harappan fire-pits may be his prehistoric ancestry; Southeast Asian fire-shrines and the homa-cults of esoteric Buddhism carried his cult across Asia.
lore.cult: The domestic āhavanīya and gārhapatya fires accompany every rite of passage; the great Śrauta agniṣṭoma lasts a year and raises the fire to the sky on a falcon-shaped brick altar. The Agnihotra prayer at dawn and dusk is his daily liturgy — three millennia without interruption.
lore.iconography: A red two-faced god — the consuming and auspicious faces — riding the ram or the goat, with seven tongues of flame and the ladle and butter in his hands. His body is flame itself; his hair the smoke; his seven tongues named in the hymns as the Kālīs, the carriers of the oblation.
lore.reception: Comparative religion uses Agni as the case where god and element are one — the purest survivorship of Indo-European fire-worship. The Roman flamen’s flame, the Zoroastrian ātaxš, and the Vedic agni form a triad scholars still trace; and the English word ‘ignite’ speaks his name in every chemistry classroom.
